definition: Fickle means changing often and without warning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fickle. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fickle should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: He was a fickle collector, obsessed with stamps in June, coins by August, and telescopes before the first frost.
Changeable is milder than fickle — changeable simply reports that something varies, while fickle adds the sting of broken trust.
Treacherous is stronger than fickle — a fickle ally merely drifts away, but a treacherous one turns and does you harm.

Flighty describes attention so scattered and impulsive that nothing gets settled on at all — flitting off before any choice is made. Fickle is about choices that do get made and then abandoned: a fickle diner had a favorite dish and dropped it; a flighty one never ordered.

Inconstant is the formal, older word for failing to stay faithful, at home in poetry and vows. Fickle is its everyday, sharper-tongued cousin: both describe loyalty that will not hold, but fickle carries the modern sting of a complaint you might actually say aloud.

Capricious behavior is governed by whim — sudden impulses that arrive from nowhere and rule the moment, as a capricious judge sentences by mood. Fickle points more narrowly at loyalty and preference that keep switching; capricious covers any decision, rule, or act driven by impulse.

Fickle's Old English family — including befician, a verb meaning 'to deceive' — died out centuries ago, leaving fickle an orphan. No common English word shares its root, so the only way in is the word itself.
Fickle means changing often and without warning.
Their manager was fickle about the schedule: the Tuesday shift she demanded all winter was suddenly wrong in April, and the plan that replaced it lasted eleven days.
Fickle is for changeability you cannot bank on, and it always carries a hint of blame — a fickle person or thing lets you down.
A sky can be changeable without offense; call it fickle and you are filing a complaint.
informal / mildly reproachful
Fickle suits everyday complaints about loyalty that will not hold — fans, appetites, luck, spring skies.

It always points a finger; if you want the fact of variation without the accusation, say changeable, and if the change is a measured rise and fall or a swing between two poles, this unit's fluctuate or oscillate is the better tool.

For three seasons, viewers could not get enough of the baking show.
Its finale drew record numbers; its catchphrases covered lunchboxes and bumper stickers.
Then, without any scandal or slump in quality, the audience simply moved on — ratings fell by half in a spring, and the lunchboxes went to clearance.
Critics shrugged and reached for an old word: audiences are fickle, they wrote, and adoration is a lease, never a deed.
The network's new hit, a pottery contest, is enjoying the same devotion now.
Its producers, reading history, have declined to celebrate.
